PUBLISHER’S NOTE 
The Puranas constitute an encyclopaedia of universal knowledge. They 
contain summaries of information on mythology, philosophy, history, geography, 
politics, economics and law. They throw light on society, religion, education, 
art and architecture of ancient and medieval India. In brief, they are the vehicles 
of liberal education devised for the masses. 


On the religious plane, they are regarded as sacred treatises. As they 
rehabilitate the ancient Vedic tradition they are called the fifth Veda. They 
are very valuable : for they are open to the masses and though they are as autho- 
ritative as the Vedas they are composed in an easily intelligible language, viz. 
the classical Sanskrit. 


But this vast literature with a growing demand for procurement has gone 
out of print. Some of the Puranas are not available at all. Others are available 
only in fragments where too the tedactor’s hand has wrought havoc in abridging 
the text in violation of the system that conceived the text as an inseparable whole. 


The present series is an attempt to present this vast literature to the reader 
in the original complete form, without disturbing the text. The series was start- 
ed in 1973, by Lala Sundarlal Jain of Messrs Motilal Banarsidass at the sugges- 
tion of Sri Narayana Svami, the scholarly saint of Calcutta. The Brahmanda 
Purana, the oldest in date and the richest in content, was published in the same 
year, in this series. The book contains the text in Devanagari, an Introduction, 
the table of contents both in Sanskrit and in English as well as an Index of Verses. 


But the sudden passing away of Sri Narayana Svami who had inspired the 
project by his saintly blessing and the untimely demise of Lala Sundarlal Jain 
who had envisaged the plan gave a set-back to the scheme and stayed the opera- 
tion of the project for a pretty long time. 


The Readers will be glad to know that we have resumed the work of printing 
the text series in right earnest and have brought out the Lingapurdana in the style 
of the Brahmanda-purdna in respect of size, binding, printing, and paper. We 
assure the readers that this style, much appreciated by the reader, will be 
maintained in the printing of subsequent volumes in the series.

INTRODUCTION 


Purana: Origin and Development 


According to Visnupurana’ the sage Krsna Dvaipayana Vyasa compiled a Purdana-sarithitg from the 
various ancient episodes and imparted the same to his disciple Romaharsana. The latter composed his own 
Purana-samhita and among his disciples Kasyapa Savarni and Sarhéapayana composed their own. 
These four were the original Purana sathhitas. This represents the first stage in the development of the 
Puranas. The Vayu purdna specifies the number of Puranas as ten. This represents the second stage. The 


traditional number eighteen is the final stage. 


The traditional list as found in the Puranas comprises the following : (1) Brahma, (2) Padma, 


(3) Visnu, (4) Vayu, (5) Bhagavata, (6) Naradiya, (7) Markandeya, (8) Agni, (9) Bhavisya, (10) Brahma- Vaivarta, 
(11) Linga, (12) Varaha, (13) Skanda, (14) Vamana, (15) Kirma, (16) Matsya, (17) Garuda, (18) Brahmanda. 


The Puranic scholars are agreed upon the authenticity of the seventeen Puranas but in regard to the 
eighteenth (No. 4 in the list) there is a difference of opinion. Majority of the Puranas include Sivapurana 


in the list while a few others substitute Vayu for Siva.2 


The Lingapurana—Contents 


The Lingapurana is divided into two Parts comprising 108 and 55 chapters respectively. 
Part I. Describes the evolution of Linga, a phallic form of Siva. It records various traditions about 


the rise of Linga cult, modes of worshipping Siva, principles of its ritual, efficacy of its worship illustrated by 
myths, legends and anecdotes. 


It provides a graphic account of the geography of the earth with seven continents, their flora and fauna, 
their people, mountains, oceans and rivers. It describes the size of the earth, stars and planets, their positions 
and movements in the heavens. It recounts the genealogies of some famous monarches of the solar and lunar 
dynasties. It gives an account of prominent Asuras, their expeditions and destruction. | 
Part II. Contains legends on the glorification of Linga, a detailed account of the form, concept and 
attributes of Linga and the Vratas, gifts and mantras related to his worship. Finally, it explains in detail the 
procedure of the Pasupata Yoga as the means of attaining the ultimate goal, viz., the absorption of the personal 


soul into the supreme soul—Lord Siva. 


The Title 


The Lingapurdna is a Saiva Purana. It derives its name from the fact that it reveals the supreme 
lord Siva in his niskala (attributeless) and sakala (qualified) forms, recounts his emblems, qualities, exploits 
and incarnations, narrates legends on the origin and importance of Linga—his phallic idol, dwells upon the 
merit of installing and consecrating it, describes the ritual and philosophical principles of the Linga cult and 


embodies sermons and dissertations on the glory of Linga.

Date of Composition 


Lingapurana reflects the fusion of old and new material which can be demarcated quite distinctly. 
There is a Vedic form of Siva-worship which seems to be definitely old as well as Its Coa mat aa 
is definitely later, Hence, we cannot fix this Purana to a definite date. The different sections of the Purana 
dealing with different topics may have been composed in different periods of time. The assimilation of this 
different material may have taken many centuries before this Purana assumed the present form after additions 
and alterations were made to it. ; 

Still we can arrive at the approximate date on the basis of the following. 

Ballalasena quotes a number of verses on omens in his Adbhutasagara which are available in the pre- 
sent text. He quotes some verses in his Danasagara too under Punyadesah and in the Zi uldpurusadana, though 
he has rejected its authority in the section on Mahadana. Since Ballala lived in 1200 A.D., the Puraga can 
not be later than that. :; 

Devanabhatta (1200—1225 A.D.) and Hemadri (1260—1270 A.D.) are the first digest-writers who cite 
verses from this Purana. This fact too points to a date not later than the twelfth century A.D. ene 

Al-Beruni (1030 A.D.) mentions this Purana in his Indica. This Purana cannot be later than 
eleventh century A.p. |
